ox: Incorrect. This is the customary view that paragraph 1 introduces only so the author can reject it ('this picture has the relationship backward').
Correct. The thesis in paragraph 1 is that instruments are 'condensed arguments'. The rest of the passage shows how the assumptions built into instruments become invisible.
Incorrect. This overshoots. Paragraph 4 says science is NOT arbitrary; the author claims hidden assumptions can be examined, not that conclusions are arbitrary.
Incorrect. Mercury thermometers are used as one example; the passage never compares accuracy between designs, so this is a detail, not the main idea.

p: The main idea is the claim the whole passage is built to support. Look for it where the author says 'I want to suggest…' or 'this picture has it backward', then check that the other paragraphs develop it. Wrong choices usually describe a detail, the view the author rejects, or an exaggeration.

xp001_0.trap: Choosing the view the author rejects (A) or an extreme restatement (C).
xp001_0.eli: The main idea is the one sentence you could say to a friend after reading: 'tools carry hidden beliefs inside them'.
mem: Main idea = the thesis the whole passage supports.
Wrong answers: a detail, the opposing view, or an extreme version.
Thesis words: 'I want to suggest', 'this is why', 'the real point'.
xp001_0.sc: Cross out any choice the author argues AGAINST, then any that is only a detail or example.
xp001_0.mn: TOD: Thesis, Opposing view, Detail: identify which one each choice is.

ox: Incorrect. Paragraph 1 lists creatures only as an opening example; the passage is about why they appear, not a catalogue.
Incorrect. Paragraph 4 says illuminators did sometimes laugh; the author argues humor and devotion can coexist.
Incorrect. The passage never describes censorship; paragraph 2 notes that patrons approved of the images.
Correct. Paragraph 2 disputes the rebellion thesis and paragraph 3 offers a devotional explanation (memory aids). Purpose = challenge a view and propose another.

concept.t: Reading the passage for what is actually argued
p: The right answer is the one the passage text directly supports. Check each choice against a specific line or paragraph; wrong choices are usually too extreme, too narrow, or not mentioned.

xp002_0.trap: Choosing a detail or example (A) as the purpose.
xp002_0.eli: A 'primary purpose' question asks what the author is DOING (arguing, challenging, proposing), not just what the passage mentions.
mem: Primary purpose = the author's job in the passage (verb: challenge, argue, explain).
Wrong answers: a mere detail, an extreme claim, or something never discussed.
Look for 'but', 'however', 'I think' to find the pivot.
xp002_0.sc: Underline the author's verb in the thesis, then match it to the choice's verb.

ox: Incorrect. Paragraph 2 offers no evidence of a secret shared rebellion; the quote doubts that the images are rebellious at all.
Correct. The remark points out that the authorities paid for and approved the images, which clashes with the idea of rebellion.
Incorrect. Paragraph 3 assigns the images a real function as memory aids, so they are more than decoration.
Incorrect. The remark is ironic criticism of the rebellion thesis, not a concession to it.

concept.t: Reading the passage for what is actually argued
p: The right answer is the one the passage text directly supports. Check each choice against a specific line or paragraph; wrong choices are usually too extreme, too narrow, or not mentioned.

xp002_1.trap: Choosing the choice that concedes the thesis (D) instead of criticizing it.
xp002_1.eli: A 'serves mainly to' question asks about the FUNCTION of a sentence in the argument.
mem: Function questions: ask what job the sentence does for the author's argument.
Ironic phrases usually criticize, not agree.
Check which paragraph the sentence sits in for context.
xp002_1.sc: Say it in your own words: 'It shows that…' then match.

ox: Incorrect. Paragraph 2 calls the honesty claim 'romantic speculation' and rejects it.
Incorrect. Paragraph 3 lists several English expressions that mark evidence, so English speakers can express it.
Correct. Paragraph 2 denies the honesty claim and paragraph 4 limits the effect to attention.
Incorrect. Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions do shape what speakers attend to, so this overstates the claim.

concept.t: Reading the passage for what is actually argued
p: The right answer is the one the passage text directly supports. Check each choice against a specific line or paragraph; wrong choices are usually too extreme, too narrow, or not mentioned.

xp003_0.trap: Choosing an extreme statement (A or D) instead of the balanced central claim.
xp003_0.eli: The central claim is usually moderate. Extreme words like 'no effect' or 'more honest' are often traps.
mem: Central claim = what the whole passage proves.
Be wary of extreme wording in choices.
The author often rejects the 'popular' view first.
xp003_0.sc: Cross out choices with absolute words, then match the thesis.

ox: Incorrect. Paragraph 2 says nothing about when either feature is acquired.
Incorrect. Paragraph 2 uses tense as an analogy, not as an evidential system.
Correct. The comparison shows that a grammatical requirement (tense or evidential marking) does not guarantee the content is true, e.g. one can use past tense for events that never happened.
Incorrect. Paragraph 2 says both choices become equally automatic, so speakers do not choose tense more carefully.

concept.t: Reading the passage for what is actually argued
p: The right answer is the one the passage text directly supports. Check each choice against a specific line or paragraph; wrong choices are usually too extreme, too narrow, or not mentioned.

xp003_1.trap: Choosing a claim the paragraph never makes.
xp003_1.eli: An analogy is used to support the author's point; find the point the two things share.
mem: Analogy questions: what do the two things have in common?
Evidential marking ≠ truthfulness.
Wrong answers add claims the passage never makes.
xp003_1.sc: Ask what the two items share, then pick the choice stating that.

ox: Wrong. The passage says 'This does not mean restoration should stop.' This option takes the author's doubts about proof and pushes them to an extreme, which is a classic overreach trap.

Correct. The passage says restoration should continue ('This does not mean restoration should stop') and that restorers owe 'candor', with labels reading 'our best current reading of it.' That is restoration plus honest labeling as interpretation.
Wrong. The passage says grime-covered paintings are 'no more authentic' than cleaned ones, only 'a record of different accidents.' This flips the author's point into the opposite extreme.

Wrong. The passage says some curators fear this, but the author 'suspects the opposite': honesty builds trust. Nothing says visitors currently distrust restoration, so this borrows a detail and distorts it.

p: The main point is the one idea the whole passage supports. Look for the author's own claim, often signaled by phrases like 'This does not mean' or 'What restorers owe.' Details and opponents' views are not the main point.
Here the author makes a claim (cleaning is guesswork), then softens it (do not stop), then gives advice (be candid). The best answer covers the advice and the limit on it.

p1_0.eli: Imagine a friend who fixes your torn drawing. It is fine that they fixed it, but they should say 'this is my best guess of what it looked like,' not 'this is exactly how you drew it.'
mem: Main point = the author's overall claim, not one detail or a rival view.
Extreme words (halt, most authentic, distrust) are often wrong.
Check each option against the exact sentence in the passage.
p1_0.sc: Write your own one-sentence summary of the passage before reading the options, then match it.
p1_0.trap: Options that take one true detail and exaggerate it, or that state an opponent's view, look attractive but are not the author's point.
p1_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage says 'Some curators object that such honesty will make visitors trust museums less. I suspect the opposite.' The author disagrees, but 'suspect' and the calm tone show respect rather than attack.
Wrong. The author directly rejects the curators' worry in the sentence 'I suspect the opposite.' Agreement would need the author to endorse the objection, which the passage never does.
Wrong. No insults or angry words appear in the passage. 'I suspect' is hedged and mild. Choosing this ignores tone and treats any disagreement as hostility.
Wrong. The author spends two sentences on the curators' objection and answers it, so the author clearly cares. Indifference would mean ignoring it.

p: Tone is shown by word choice. Strong, harsh words suggest anger. Hedged words like 'I suspect' or 'perhaps' suggest a measured, polite view.
On MCAT tone questions, the right answer usually matches the passage's strength. Extreme choices like 'open hostility' or 'complete agreement' are usually too strong.

p1_1.eli: If your friend says 'we should skip homework,' and you say 'Hmm, I think the opposite,' you disagree but you are being polite. You did not yell at them.
mem: Hedge words (suspect, perhaps) signal measured, mild tone.
Pick the attitude with the same strength as the passage.
Indifference is wrong if the author directly answers the other side.
p1_1.trap: Extreme tone words are tempting, but a calm disagreement is 'respectful,' not 'hostile.'
p1_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Like the author's advice to label restoration as 'our best current reading,' the historian admits a reconstruction is one plausible version. Both are rebuilding something lost and being candid about uncertainty.
Wrong. The author says restoration should not stop ('This does not mean restoration should stop'). Refusing to rebuild matches the view the author rejects, not the recommendation.
Wrong. Printing with no edits has no reconstruction and no honest disclosure of guesswork, so it misses both parts of the author's advice (restore, and be candid).
Wrong. Claiming exact fidelity to 1700 is the overclaim the author attacks, like 'restored to its original state.' This matches the practice being criticized.

p: An application question asks you to carry the author's principle into a new setting. First state the principle in plain words, then find the option with the same structure.
Here the principle is: reconstruct the past when needed, but be honest that it is an informed interpretation, not a certainty.

p1_2.eli: A friend draws a dinosaur from bones and says 'this is what scientists think it looked like.' That is honest. Saying 'this is exactly how it looked' is not.
mem: Restate the author's principle first, then match structure, not topic.
The author wants both: keep restoring AND be candid about uncertainty.
Options that copy the criticized behavior are traps.
p1_2.trap: Picking an option that shares the topic (old things) but not the principle of honest labeling.
p1_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. The passage never says paved paths make people ignore signs. Signs are only mentioned as the old standard response (sentence 3). This is an outside-the-passage trap.

Correct. Paragraph 1, sentences 'Its limits are less discussed. Paths record where people already go, not where they might go if the space offered something better.' The limit is that paths capture current habits, not better possibilities.
Wrong. The passage never mentions cost for paving or fencing. Choosing it means you imported your own assumption.
Wrong. The year of waiting is described as part of the method (they 'waited a year'), not as a limitation the author raises. Do not confuse a description with a criticism.

p: A 'limitation' question asks what the author says is the weakness of an idea. Look for signal words such as 'limits', 'however', or 'but'. The author usually states the weakness directly right after.
Here, the signal is 'Its limits are less discussed.' The next sentence gives the answer: paths only show where people already walk.

p2_0.eli: If you only ever order the pizza your friends already like, you never find out about a better kind.
mem: Signal words like 'limits' or 'however' point to the author's critique.
The right answer paraphrases the passage text; wrong ones add new ideas like cost.
Past habits are not the same as future possibilities.
p2_0.trap: Picking an answer that sounds like a plausible criticism but is never mentioned in the passage (cost, signs).
p2_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The final claim says a plan that ignores observed behavior 'will be quietly redrawn by it'. If sites that ignored walking patterns stayed intact with no worn paths for decades, the prediction fails. It directly contradicts the claim.
Wrong. Liking paved paths fits the author's view that observed behavior should guide design. It supports the author or is neutral, so it cannot weaken the claim.
Wrong. The length of some paths says nothing about whether ignored behavior leads to redrawn plans. It is irrelevant to the claim.
Wrong. Other countries using fences is about what planners do, not the outcome the author predicts. It does not test the claim.

p: To weaken a claim, first restate exactly what the author predicts. Then find the answer that shows the prediction is false or unlikely.
The author predicts: ignore observed behavior, and people will redraw the plan. A result where plans were ignored but nothing changed breaks that cause-and-effect link.

p2_1.eli: If someone says 'if you leave the door unlocked, the cat will get out' and you find a house with an open door where the cat stayed in for years, the claim looks weak.
mem: Weaken: attack the stated outcome, not the topic.
Irrelevant details and supporting facts are never the answer.
Look for the choice that gives the opposite result under the same conditions.
p2_1.trap: Choosing a choice that is merely on topic (fences, path length) instead of one that tests the author's predicted outcome.
p2_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The sentence says feet are treated 'as data rather than defiance'. Defiance is what planners used to see in corner-cutters, a deliberate refusal to follow the intended route, as shown by the fence-or-sign response.
Wrong. Walking on grass wears it down, but defiance here is about attitude toward rules, not damage. This is a too-narrow reading.
Wrong. Careful planning is the architects' approach, not what the walkers are accused of. It is the opposite sense.
Wrong. Protest is organized and public. Cutting a corner is much milder, so this overstates the meaning.

p: Words in CARS are tested for the meaning they have in the passage, not a dictionary meaning. Read the sentence around the word and see what it contrasts with.
'Data rather than defiance' contrasts two ways to see the worn path: as useful information, or as rule-breaking.

p2_2.eli: When a kid cuts across the yard, a grumpy neighbor calls it naughty, while a smart neighbor says 'that is just the fastest way.'
mem: Use the contrast words ('rather than') to find meaning.
Pick the choice with the right strength, not too extreme.
Test by plugging each choice into the sentence.
p2_2.trap: Picking the extreme choices (property damage, protest) that overstate the mild behavior of walking on grass.
p2_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage says composers' own metronome markings are now considered unplayable or mistaken, and concludes 'the numbers may have promised more precision than music can bear.' That conclusion only works if the composers' markings would be right when precise markings truly suit music. If precision did suit music, their own numbers should have worked.

Wrong. The passage (sentence 5, 'Yet several composers' own metronome markings...') says 'several' markings are unplayable, not all. This is the extreme-word trap: 'all' turns a modest claim into an absolute one.
Wrong. The passage's final sentences say 'None of this makes tempo arbitrary.' The author states the opposite. Do not confuse 'precision is limited' with 'tempo does not matter'.

Wrong. The passage (sentence 4) says some historians celebrate precise markings as progress, so they are not described as disliking them. The author only hints at skepticism ('Yet several...') and never says historians dislike metronomes. This option reverses a detail from the passage.

p: An assumption is an unstated idea the argument needs to be true. The author gives evidence and a conclusion, but does not spell out the link between them.

Test it: if the assumption were false, would the argument fall apart? Here the evidence is that composers' own precise markings fail. For that to show precision does not fit music, the composers' markings must otherwise be reliable.

p3_0.eli: If the person who wrote a recipe cannot cook it the way it says, maybe the recipe asked for too much exactness. That only makes sense if the writer knew what they wanted.
mem: An assumption fills the gap between evidence and conclusion.
Negate the choice: if the argument breaks, it is the assumption.
Extreme words like 'all' and 'never' are usually wrong in CARS.
p3_0.sc: Ask: what must be true for this evidence to support this conclusion? Then check the choice against that.
p3_0.trap: Picking an extreme or reversed statement ('all', 'dislike') that sounds related but is not needed by the argument.
p3_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reasoning skills; checked against the passage text provided, not against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The last sentence says a score is 'closer to an argument than a blueprint, and that a performance answers it rather than executes it.' A blueprint is built exactly as drawn. An argument is answered with a response. So the score invites interpretation, not exact copying.
Wrong. The author says 'None of this makes tempo arbitrary,' so the score still matters. This is the too-extreme trap: the passage says precision is limited, not that the score is useless.
Wrong. The passage never compares scores with recordings. Nothing in any paragraph ranks their value. This is an out-of-scope trap.

Wrong. This is the blueprint view, which the author argues against with the line 'closer to an argument than a blueprint.' A blueprint is executed exactly; the author says a performance does not simply execute.

p: An analogy compares two things to show one shared idea. Ask what each thing is like and which side the author favors.
A blueprint is followed exactly. An argument is something you respond to. The author says a score is the second kind, so performers respond to it with their own reading.

p3_1.eli: A blueprint is like a Lego manual: follow every step. An argument is like a question from a friend: you answer it your own way.
mem: Blueprint means exact execution.
Argument means a response or interpretation.
The author sides with the 'argument' view.
p3_1.trap: Choosing 'must be followed precisely,' which is the view the author rejects.
p3_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reasoning skills; checked against the passage text provided, not against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The last sentences say the useful question is 'Faithful to what, and at what cost?' and that a translator who can answer it clearly 'has done the real work.' That makes clear reasoning about priorities and trade-offs the standard.
Wrong. Sentences 3-4 say staying close to the words is only one kind of faithfulness, and it can sound stiff. The trap is treating 'literal' as the same as 'faithful.'

Wrong. The final clause says the translator has done the real work 'even if critics disagree with the answer.' So critic approval is not the test. The trap is picking an answer that sounds like a common standard but that the author sets aside.
Wrong. The passage says readers tend to praise the first translation they read, and treats this as a bias from familiarity (sentence 5). Being first is not evidence of quality.

concept.t: Judging by reasoning, not by a single standard
p: The author says 'faithful' is vague. A translation can be faithful to the exact words or faithful to the natural feel. You cannot have both fully, so every translator gives something up.
So the author wants us to judge the translator's choices: what did they put first, what did they give up, and can they explain why? A trade-off is a choice where gaining one thing costs another.

p4_0.eli: It is like a cook asked 'Is the dish tasty?' A better question is 'What did you aim for, and what did you give up to get it?'
mem: In CARS, find the author's own proposed standard; it is usually stated near the end.
Wrong options often take one side of a trade-off the author says is incomplete.
Words like 'even if critics disagree' show the author rejects outside approval as the test.
p4_0.trap: Choosing 'literal match' because faithful sounds like word-for-word. The author explicitly calls literal faithfulness only one kind.
p4_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reading-comprehension practice; based only on the passage given, not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Sentence 5 says readers praise the first translation they read, 'which suggests that familiarity, not accuracy, shapes much of our judgment.' The claim is there to show that familiarity can bias judgments of accuracy.
Wrong. The author uses the claim to cast doubt on that praise, saying familiarity, not accuracy, drives it. The trap is reading 'praise' as the author's own endorsement.
Wrong. The passage never argues against translating classics. It is only about how translations should be judged. The trap is bringing in an outside conclusion the text never draws.

Wrong. The author says readers are influenced by familiarity, a natural bias, not that they are careless. The words 'much of our judgment' include everyone ('our'), and the tone is not accusing. This option is too strong.

concept.t: Function of a detail in the passage
p: A 'function' question asks why the author included a sentence, not what it says. Look at the words right after it. Here 'which suggests that...' tells you the purpose.
Familiarity bias means we like what we know first, even if it is not better. The author uses this to show that our judgments of translations are not purely about accuracy.

p4_1.eli: You think the first pizza place you ever tried is the best, just because it is the one you know. Your liking comes from habit, not from taste tests.
mem: For function questions, read the phrase that follows the detail, such as 'which suggests.'
Reject options that make the author more extreme, like 'careless' or 'prove.'
Match the claim's role: here it is evidence of bias.
p4_1.trap: Picking 'readers are careless,' which sounds close but is harsher than the author's gentle point about bias.
p4_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reading-comprehension practice; based only on the passage given, not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage opens by describing the solitary-hero story, then says 'The record is messier,' and ends by saying the story 'hides the shared groundwork.' Every sentence serves that one point.
The author blocks this exact reading: 'This is not a case for dismissing talent. Some individuals clearly see further.' The trap is turning a limited claim into an extreme one.
Prizes show up once ('hand one person a prize') as part of how the hero story flatters institutions. One passing mention is not the main purpose, and 'corrupt' is never claimed.
Instruments appear only in a list of shared resources rivals used ('the same instruments'). The trap is picking a detail and calling it the topic.

p: The main purpose is the one job the whole passage does. Ask: what is the author trying to get me to believe? Look at the first claim, the turn (words like 'but' or 'the record is messier'), and the last sentence.
Wrong choices are usually too extreme, too narrow (one detail), or about a different topic.

p5_0.eli: It is like a team winning a game, but the news only talks about the player who scored. The author says the whole team, coaches, and field mattered too.
mem: Main idea = the claim that the first and last sentences both support.
Extreme words like 'prove,' 'no role,' 'corrupt' are usually wrong.
A detail or example is not the main purpose.
p5_0.sc: Read the first and last sentences. Here the last one names the 'lone-genius story' hiding 'shared groundwork,' which matches choice A almost word for word.
p5_0.trap: Choices B and C turn a measured argument into an extreme one. The author even says talent is not being dismissed.
p5_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage says rivals reached ideas 'within months of one another' from 'the same published results, the same instruments,' and concludes it is 'hard to argue that the idea depended on one exceptional mind.' So shared conditions matter more.
The passage never says anyone copied. Rivals reached ideas independently from the same public materials. The trap is mixing up 'same sources' with 'stealing.'
Accident is never mentioned. The author's point is that the groundwork made the discoveries likely, which is the opposite of luck.
This reverses the text. The rivals worked from 'published results,' so results were being published.

p: These questions ask what a fact is being used to prove. Find the fact in the passage, then find the sentence right after it that draws a conclusion.
Here the fact is several people arriving at the same idea at about the same time. The conclusion is that the idea did not need one special mind.

p5_1.eli: If five kids in different homes all build the same Lego castle after the store sells the same set, the set made it possible. It was not one kid's magic.
mem: Ask: what conclusion does the author draw right after the fact?
Stay inside the text; do not add motives like copying or luck.
Reversal choices flip what the passage said.
p5_1.trap: Choice B sounds plausible from outside knowledge about rivalry, but the passage never claims copying.
p5_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The last sentence says the lone-genius belief makes the public 'less willing to pay for that groundwork.' Shared labs, data sets, and instruments are that groundwork, so the author would want them funded.
Bigger prizes for single people would strengthen the hero story the author is criticizing. The trap is that prizes are mentioned, so they feel on topic.
Too extreme. The author only says prizes are something the story lets institutions do; there is no call to end them. Watch for 'all' and 'ending.'
The author says the hero narrative is the problem. Teaching only biographies would push that story even harder, and 'only' is another extreme word.

p: Application questions ask you to carry the author's view into a new situation. First state the author's view in one line, then pick the choice that fits it.
Here the view is: the hidden shared groundwork is undervalued, and the hero story is why.

p5_2.eli: If you think a pizza needs the farmers, truck drivers, and oven and not just the chef, you would want to pay for all of them, not only give the chef a trophy.
mem: Restate the author's view first, then test each choice against it.
Reject choices that strengthen what the author criticizes.
Extreme words ('all,' 'only,' 'ending') are red flags.
p5_2.trap: Choice B and C both use the word 'prize,' which is a word-match lure. Match the idea, not the word.
p5_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage says the patrons' grief is 'understandable' (sympathy), but 'rests on a narrow idea of what a library is for' (does not agree). Both halves of the answer match the same sentence.
Scornful means contempt. The author calls the grief 'understandable', which is the opposite of mocking it. The trap is reading 'narrow idea' as an insult when it is a mild, reasoned criticism.
Fully persuaded would mean the author agrees with the mourners. The author says their view is a 'mistake' in the last sentence. The trap is stopping after the sympathetic phrase.
Indifferent means not caring. The author names the patrons and answers their view directly, so the author does engage. The trap is confusing a calm tone with no opinion.

p: Tone is how the author feels about a subject. Look for evaluative words, like 'understandable' or 'mistake'. These show feelings.
Many authors mix feelings. Here the author is kind to the people but disagrees with the idea. The best answer must capture both parts.

p6_0.eli: It is like telling a friend, 'I get why you are sad your favorite park changed, but I think the new playground is a good thing.'
mem: Find the evaluative words, not the facts.
Mixed attitudes are common; pick the answer that holds both sides.
Extreme words (scornful, fully, indifferent) are usually wrong.
p6_0.sc: Quote the key phrase 'understandable but rests on a narrow idea' and match it to the option with both sympathy and disagreement.
p6_0.trap: Extreme answers that capture only one half of the author's mixed attitude.
p6_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage is one paragraph, so the claim here is the argument that libraries serve people with crowded homes (sentences 4-5: silence served readers with quiet homes, but crowded homes make the library the only place to print, get internet and let a child learn). For this to support noisy libraries, the author must assume libraries should prioritize people who lack alternatives.
The author never says silence harms reading. The author says a good library can still protect quiet. The trap is confusing 'quiet is not the whole mission' with 'quiet is bad'.
The passage never mentions borrowing numbers. Cafes are listed only as an example of change. The trap is picking an option that sounds library-related but has no support in the text.
The passage says children can learn 'among other children', not that quiet blocks learning. This reverses a mild claim into an extreme one.

p: An assumption is an unstated idea the argument needs in order to work. If you removed it, the argument would fall apart.
Ask: what must be true for the author's reasons to lead to the conclusion? Here the reasons are about who lacks other places. Name the claim by its content, since the passage is a single paragraph.

p6_1.eli: If you say 'the last cookie should go to the kid who got none,' you assume that fairness to the one with nothing matters.
mem: Assumption = missing link between reason and conclusion.
Negate the option: if the argument breaks, it is the assumption.
Wrong options are often never mentioned or too extreme.
p6_1.sc: Negation test: 'Libraries should NOT serve the least-resourced' would undercut the argument.
p6_1.trap: Choosing a statement the passage never makes, or an exaggerated version of what it says.
p6_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The final sentences say a good library can still protect quiet and that quiet is 'one service among several'. Soundproof rooms next to a busy children's area offer both, which fits exactly.
The author supports mixed uses and wants quiet kept as one service. Adding quiet rooms is not a betrayal. The trap is thinking the author opposes quiet itself.
The author rejects the idea that quiet is 'the whole mission'. Quiet rooms alongside noisy areas show the opposite. The trap is taking the mourners' side.
It applies directly, because the scenario is about balancing quiet and noise, the very topic of the argument. Calling it irrelevant ignores the passage's last two sentences.

concept.t: Applying the passage to a new case
p: Beyond-the-text questions give a new situation. Find the author's principle, then check which option follows it.
The principle here: quiet is one service among several. A library with both quiet rooms and busy areas matches it.

p6_2.eli: A school with both a loud playground and a quiet reading corner is giving kids more than one thing they need.
mem: State the author's principle in one line first.
The answer should agree with the author's main point.
Reject options that flip the author's stance.
p6_2.sc: Restate the thesis, then pick the option that sounds like it.
p6_2.trap: Assuming the author is anti-quiet when the author only says quiet is not the sole goal.
p6_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Sentences 5-6 say 'Both accounts treat the viewer as passive' and 'Yet the feeling depends heavily on what the viewer brings.' The objection is that the accounts leave out the viewer's own contribution.
Wrong. The passage never says the accounts are factually false. The author only says they are incomplete. Trap: mistaking 'objection' for 'says it is wrong'.
Wrong. The passage never discusses complete temples being overly beautiful. It only says a complete temple 'impresses' in the first sentence. Trap: grabbing a detail from the opening line.
Wrong. Nothing limits the accounts to ancient ruins. Trap: adding a restriction the author never makes.

p: When a passage says 'Both accounts...Yet...', the word 'Yet' marks the author's turn. What comes after 'Yet' is the author's own point.
Here the accounts say the stones cause the feeling. The author says the viewer helps cause it. So the objection is that the viewer's role is ignored.

p7_0.eli: Imagine two people say a movie is sad only because of the music. You say, 'But what you remember and feel matters too.' They forgot you.
mem: 'Yet' or 'But' after a view signals the author's objection.
An objection is usually 'this leaves something out', not 'this is false'.
Wrong CARS choices often invent claims the passage never makes.
p7_0.sc: Find the sentence right after the criticized views and ask what it adds. That added piece is what they ignored.
p7_0.trap: Choosing 'historically inaccurate' because objections feel like 'wrong'. The author calls the accounts incomplete, not inaccurate.
p7_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reasoning skills; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The last sentence says restoring 'removes the space our stories filled.' Earlier, the passage says ruins invite imagination and that the emotion is 'a story we tell.' The space is the missing parts where viewers imagine and interpret.
Wrong. This reads 'space' as literal rooms. The passage is about imagination, not architecture. Trap: taking a figurative phrase literally.
Wrong. Museum cases appear nowhere in the passage. Trap: bringing in outside ideas.

Wrong. The stories are the viewer's own ('a story we tell about it'), not written histories. The passage actually says a visitor may know nothing of the builders. Trap: confusing 'story' with 'history'.

p: Figurative language means words used for an idea, not literally. 'Space our stories filled' is figurative.
To decode it, find the nearby literal idea. The passage says ruins invite imagination and the emotion is a story we tell. So the 'space' is the gap left by missing stone, where imagination works.

p7_1.eli: A coloring book with some parts left blank lets you add your own colors. Filling every part in takes away your fun.
mem: Decode a metaphor by finding the literal idea in nearby sentences.
Reject answers that make a metaphor literal.
Reject answers that bring in things not in the passage.
p7_1.trap: Picking 'physical rooms' because 'space' sounds physical. The surrounding sentences are about imagination.
p7_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reasoning skills; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The author claims the feeling 'depends heavily on what the viewer brings' (sentence 6). If knowing a site's history, which the viewer brings, raises the emotion, that directly supports the claim.
Wrong. Taking photos says nothing about where the emotion comes from. Trap: choosing a popular-sounding fact that is off-topic.
Wrong. Tourism numbers do not measure emotion. And the last paragraph says restoring can disappoint, so this leans the other way. Trap: an answer that sounds relevant but does not test the claim.
Wrong. Age of ruins has no link to the claim about the viewer's role. Trap: a true-sounding detail that is irrelevant.

p: To strengthen a claim, pick the evidence that would make it more likely true. First state the claim in your own words.
Here the claim is: the viewer's own knowledge and stories shape the emotion. Evidence that changing what the viewer knows changes the emotion fits.

p7_2.eli: If you say a joke is funnier when you know the backstory, the best proof is that people told the backstory laugh more.
mem: First restate the author's claim, then test each choice against it.
Strong evidence changes the cause and shows the effect changes.
Irrelevant facts, even true ones, do not strengthen.
p7_2.trap: Choosing an answer that is merely about ruins. It must link to the viewer's contribution.
p7_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS reasoning skills; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The passage says a number tied to rewards 'starts to change the behavior it was meant to describe' and gives two examples (the clinic and the surgeon). The last sentences say the metric is only a proxy.

Wrong. This is the trap of reading the problems and missing the solution. The last paragraph line says 'The answer is not to stop counting,' and the passage also says measurement 'caught real failures.'
Wrong. Patient ratings are only listed as one of several metrics in the first sentence. The passage never ranks them or calls them reliable. This is an unsupported claim.
Wrong. This is an extreme reading. The surgeon avoids sick patients because of the reward tied to survival rates. The passage blames incentives, not bad character.

p: The central claim is the one idea the whole passage supports. Check it against every part: the examples, the turn ('But...'), and the closing advice.
A good answer covers all of that. A wrong answer is often too extreme, too narrow (only one example), or not in the passage at all.

p8_0.eli: If a teacher pays you for every book you finish, you may pick tiny picture books. You finish more books, but you read less. The reward changed what you do.
mem: Central claim = covers the whole passage, not one example.
Extreme words (stop, most, dishonest) are usually wrong.
The author's last lines often state the main point.
p8_0.sc: Find the 'But' or 'However' sentence. The main claim usually sits right after it.
p8_0.trap: Choosing an extreme option like 'stop measuring' or 'surgeons are dishonest' that the author explicitly avoids.
p8_0.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The surgeon avoids the sickest patients, so survival rates rise. The passage then says 'the measure improves while the thing it stood for may get worse.' That is this exact point.
Wrong. The passage says the sickest operations are 'riskiest but most needed.' It is not claiming surgery is too dangerous. Danger is a detail, not the purpose of the example.
Wrong. Wait times belong to the clinic example, the one just before the surgeon. This choice mixes up the two examples.
Wrong. The passage says measurement 'caught real failures that intuition missed.' It credits measurement, so this reverses the author's view.

p: An example is there to prove a point the author already made. Ask: what general claim is this example backing?
Here the general claim is that a rewarded number can improve while real quality drops. The surgeon is one case of that.

p8_1.eli: A student who only takes easy tests gets a perfect average. The average looks great, but they did not learn more.
mem: Examples serve the claim near them.
Match each option to the right example (clinic = waits, surgeon = survival).
Check the option does not reverse the author's view.
p8_1.trap: Picking an option that belongs to a different example or flips what the author said about measurement.
p8_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Adjusting for how sick patients were removes the reward for avoiding them. The metric stays tied to what it stands for (good care), which is what the author asks for.
Wrong. This rewards short visits, which is the clinic example where visits get rushed. It repeats the distortion the author warns about.
Wrong. The author says 'The answer is not to stop counting.' Dropping all metrics is directly rejected.
Wrong. Patient ratings are just another proxy. Using only one proxy with no check on what it stands for ignores the author's advice to keep asking what it is a proxy for.

p: Application questions ask you to take the author's principle and use it on a new case. First state the principle in your own words.
Here it is: keep measuring, but keep checking that each metric still reflects the real goal. Pick the option that does both.

p8_2.eli: If a game scores only speed, players will cheat on accuracy. A fair score also checks how hard the level was.
mem: Advice = keep counting AND question the proxy.
Wrong options either repeat the problem or throw out measurement.
Restate the principle before reading options.
p8_2.trap: Choosing 'abolish metrics' (too extreme) or swapping one proxy for another without any check.
p8_2.academic: Written from standard MCAT CARS strategy knowledge; not checked against a live AAMC document.
